1. Scientific Analysis

Analysis Type

Nanoparticle detection and size distribution via scale-space LoG blob detection (log_blob_detect, ~80 nm) with distance-transform watershed splitting of touching particles; equivalent-circle diameters measured from a single consistent labeled-region step (region area).

Interpretation

The analysis measures the size distribution of spherical Au nanoparticles imaged by TEM at a calibrated pixel size of 0.3955 nm/px (810 nm field of view). Particles appear as dark, densely-packed discs; watershed splitting of the Otsu foreground mask resolved 101 labeled regions, of which 88 are interior (non-border) particles usable for unbiased sizing. The interior equivalent-circle diameter distribution is tightly unimodal, centered at a median of 73.7 nm (mean 74.2 nm) with a standard deviation of 2.5 nm, giving a polydispersity (std/mean) of ~3.4%. Physically, this low polydispersity indicates a highly monodisperse colloidal synthesis — the particles are nearly uniform in size, consistent with a well-controlled seeded-growth or citrate-type Au sphere preparation. The high median solidity (0.985) confirms the segmented regions are convex, filled discs (no concave fragments), and the unimodal histogram with no cluster of sub-quarter-area fragments indicates the watershed did not over-segment into spurious pieces. The lower circularity median (0.76) reflects mild boundary irregularity introduced by the segmentation at contact points between touching particles rather than true particle faceting. Two known biases temper the absolute size value: (1) the equivalent-circle diameter is measured ~8% below the 80 nm nominal because the dark particle rim and bright inter-particle gaps erode the Otsu-segmented area, imposing a consistent low bias across all particles; and (2) the recovered count (88 interior, 101 total) is below the ~120-140 visually present, so some tightly-touching particles were merged or missed. Crucially, both biases act systematically and do not affect the relative width of the distribution, so the polydispersity estimate is robust even though the absolute mean is slightly underestimated. For the stated objective — measuring the size distribution — the dominant, reliable finding is that the population is monodisperse near 74-80 nm.

3. Scientific Claims

Claim 1: The Au nanoparticle population is highly monodisperse, with an interior equivalent-circle diameter of 73.7 nm (median; mean 74.2 nm) and a polydispersity (std/mean) of ~3.4% (std 2.5 nm) across 88 interior particles; the absolute diameter is a slight (~8%) systematic underestimate of the 80 nm nominal size due to segmentation-area erosion at dark rims.

Scientific Impact: Low polydispersity (<5%) is the key quality metric for colloidal Au syntheses used in plasmonics, catalysis, and biosensing, where optical/reactive properties depend sharply on uniform size; this confirms a well-controlled synthesis and validates the batch for size-sensitive applications.

Literature Search Query: Has anyone measured a size polydispersity below 5% for ~80 nm spherical Au nanoparticles by quantitative TEM image analysis?

Keywords: gold nanoparticles, size distribution, polydispersity, TEM, monodisperse colloid, equivalent-circle diameter

4. Caveats & Limitations

Absolute diameter is systematically ~8% low: the Otsu/watershed segmented area under-measures because dark particle rims and bright inter-particle gaps erode the foreground region — the true median is likely closer to the 80 nm nominal. Particle recall is incomplete: 101 detected (88 interior) versus ~120-140 visually present in the dense field, so tightly-touching particles were merged or missed; this reduces sampling but, being a random loss, does not bias the size distribution shape. Circularity (0.76) is depressed by segmentation boundary artifacts at contact points, not by real particle non-sphericity. Interior-only statistics (border particles excluded) are the correct basis for sizing and avoid truncation bias.
